cards.title: Concert ticket drop
cards.prompt: Design the ticketing system for a stadium concert: sixty thousand seats, and about three million fans trying to buy the moment sales open at ten in the morning.
facts_if_asked: A seat hold lasts eight minutes while the fan pays.
Payments go through a third party processor that answers in one to five seconds and calls back with the result.
At most four tickets per account.
Most fans arrive in the first two minutes; the event usually sells out in about twenty.
Overselling a seat is unacceptable; showing a seat that just went is tolerable.
Fans are mostly on phones.
follow_ups: How do you guarantee two fans never get the same seat?
What does the fan see while they wait?
The payment callback arrives twice. What happens?
One event is a hot partition. How do you spread the load?
How do bots change your design?
cards.twist: Sales open and the seat map service starts timing out. What degrades, and what do fans see?
strong_answer_covers: Numbers: peak arrival rate, reads far above writes, sixty thousand writes total
Virtual waiting room or admission queue to meter fans into the purchase flow
Seat hold with an expiry and an atomic conditional write, so a seat moves from free to held only once
Idempotent payment callbacks keyed by an order id; release holds on failure or timeout
Seat map reads served from a cache or snapshot, separate from the write path
Load shedding and a fair queue order; bot defence at admission
red_flags: Relies on a cache as the source of truth for seat ownership
Says the database will handle three million users without any queue or numbers

cards.title: Food truck finder
cards.prompt: Design an app that shows people the open food trucks near them. Each truck's phone reports its location every thirty seconds.
brief_lines: Users see open trucks near them
facts_if_asked: About fifty thousand trucks across many cities, about twenty thousand active at lunch peak.
About two million daily users; peak of five thousand searches per second at lunch.
Near means within two kilometres by default.
A truck that stops reporting for two minutes should disappear.
Results should feel fresh within a minute.
follow_ups: Which index do you use to find nearby trucks, and why?
A truck's phone goes offline. What does the user see?
Writes or reads: which one dominates, and does it matter?
How would you add menus and photos?
cards.twist: A festival puts four hundred trucks in one square kilometre. What breaks first?
strong_answer_covers: Write rate: about seven hundred location updates per second at peak, small payloads
Geohash or grid cells, or a spatial index, in an in memory store
Time to live on positions so stale trucks drop out
Write path separate from read path; reads served from the in memory index
Static data like menus in a database with a cache and object storage for photos
Hot cell handling: finer cells or a cap and ranking of results
red_flags: Scans every truck in a relational table for each search with no index

cards.title: Team chat with read receipts
cards.prompt: Design a team chat app with group conversations and read receipts that show who has read each message.
facts_if_asked: Ten million daily active users.
Groups of up to five hundred members; most are under twenty.
About forty messages per user per day.
Messages must arrive in the same order for everyone in a conversation.
Users who were offline get everything when they come back.
Delivery should feel instant, under a second when online.
follow_ups: How does a message reach a user who is online right now?
How do you keep ordering within a conversation?
What do read receipts cost in a five hundred person group?
A gateway server dies with a hundred thousand open connections. What happens?
cards.twist: Product wants to show read receipts per message for every group size. What does that cost, and what would you push back with?
strong_answer_covers: Rough numbers: about four hundred million messages a day, a few thousand per second at peak
Persistent connections through a gateway layer, with a registry of who is connected where
Per conversation sequence numbers for ordering; store then forward
Offline delivery from storage by last seen sequence number
Receipts stored as a last read pointer per member, batched, instead of one record per message per reader
Reconnect storms handled with backoff and resume from the last sequence number
red_flags: Writes a receipt row for every message for every member of large groups without noticing the cost

cards.title: Notification hub
cards.prompt: Design the notification system for a ride app: push, text message and email, respecting each user's preferences and quiet hours, and never sending duplicates.
facts_if_asked: About five hundred million notifications a day, peaks of twenty thousand per second during evening rush.
Some are urgent, like your driver is here; most are not, like receipts and promotions.
Urgent ones should arrive within five seconds.
SMS and email go through outside providers with rate limits and occasional outages.
Quiet hours never apply to urgent ride updates.
follow_ups: How do you avoid sending the same notification twice?
An SMS provider goes down for ten minutes. What happens?
Where do preferences and quiet hours get checked?
How do you keep promotions from delaying urgent messages?
cards.twist: Retries after a provider timeout are causing users to get duplicate texts. Walk me through the fix.
strong_answer_covers: Event intake through a durable queue
Preference and quiet hours check before fan out to channels
Idempotency key per notification, recorded before or atomically with the send
Per channel workers with backoff, and failover to a second provider
Separate priority lanes so urgent traffic never waits behind bulk
Delivery status tracking and a dead letter path
red_flags: Calls providers synchronously from the ride service with no queue
Claims exactly once delivery from an outside provider with no idempotency story

cards.title: Live quiz leaderboard
cards.prompt: Design the backend for a live quiz show in an app. Players answer each question within ten seconds, and after every question everyone sees the top hundred and their own rank.
brief_lines: After each question: top 100 and your own rank
facts_if_asked: About two million concurrent players at peak.
Fifteen questions per show, one show a day.
Answers after the ten second window don't count; the client clock can't be trusted.
Score is points per correct answer, faster answers earn more.
Ranks can be a few seconds late but must be right.
follow_ups: Two million answers arrive in ten seconds. How do you take them in?
How do you compute each player's exact rank?
How do you stop late answers from players with tampered clocks?
What happens if the scoring service falls behind?
cards.twist: Product wants ranks within friend groups as well as globally. What changes?
strong_answer_covers: Burst math: about two hundred thousand answers per second for ten seconds
Accept answers into a queue or partitioned log, timestamped by the server
Score in parallel by partition, then merge
Sorted set or bucketed counts for ranks; exact rank via counts above a score
Top hundred cached and pushed; own rank fetched or pushed per player
Graceful degradation: delayed ranks rather than lost answers
red_flags: Sorts two million players from scratch on every request
